show: Speak Up: Develop Your Executive Presence & Leadership Communication Style
titel: 622: To Rescue Your Executive Presence from the Dumpster Fire Stop Doing These 5 Things (from the 2026 Executive Influence Index)

faehigkeiten.grund: Dynamik weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen: keine Merkmale gefunden, aber eine unveraenderte Wiederholungsprobe beweist nichts

einzeiler: Five habits holding back your executive presence and how to fix them for better influence.
kurzfassung: High-performing leaders often damage their executive presence by over-communicating and trying to prove how smart they are. Based on research from the executive influence index, Laura Camacho outlines five behaviors to eliminate, including sharing too much information and being overly agreeable. Instead of acting as mere subject matter experts, leaders should evolve into interpreters and advisors by asking strategic questions.
stichpunkte: Avoid sharing everything you know; focus strictly on what the audience needs for decision-making.
Stop anticipating and answering every possible objection within the presentation itself.
Shift from trying to prove intelligence to highlighting others and asking strategic questions.
Eliminate false harmony and replace blind agreeability with productive friction and respectful challenge.
Banish boredom from meetings through storytelling, analogies, and unexpected elements.
Progress professionally from a technical expert to an interpreter and finally a trusted advisor.

kapitel.titel: Stop Trying to Prove You Belong

clips.hook: Nobody cares about everything you know
clips.text: High performers struggle with sharing their extensive analysis because they are rewarded for deep preparation, but audiences only care about how information impacts them.

clips.hook: Why answering every question in advance ruins presentations
clips.text: Presenters often overload slide decks with preemptive answers, only for audience members to raise their hands and ask the exact same questions moments later.

clips.hook: A master twist to upgrade your meeting questions
clips.text: Asking what conditions must exist for a specific strategy to succeed stimulates critical thinking in the room far better than making a standard recommendation.

clips.hook: Driving harmoniously off a cliff together
clips.text: When teams prioritize politeness and team play above all else, absolute politeness can inadvertently lead a group to catastrophic outcomes.

clips.hook: Boredom is never a business asset
clips.text: Endless boring meetings drain participants who feel trapped with no escape, yet lethargy offers zero value to any organization.

beschreibung:
Know Your Own Executive Presence Strengths & Opportunities:
Click here to pinpoint the specific area in your executive presence that’s keeping you invisible to senior leadership and guarantees you stay working hard as a pack mule who never gets promoted.

What if the behaviors you think make you look hardworking, prepared, and smart are actually making you look less executive? It happens more often than you think.

High performers are often rewarded for knowing more, doing more, explaining more, and working harder. But as you move into senior leadership, those same habits can start working against you. Executive influence isn't about producing the most output—it’s about knowing what matters, communicating it clearly, and creating better thinking and decisions around you.

In this episode of Speak Up, Dr. Laura Camacho reveals seven things you can stop doing at work to strengthen your executive presence and make the transition from expert to interpreter, advisor, and executive.

By the end of this episode you’ll know how to:

🏆Communicate with greater authority by saying less, prioritizing what matters, and eliminating unnecessary information

🏹Strengthen your influence by asking sharper questions, creating productive friction, and focusing less on proving you’re the smartest person in the room

🪝Increase your executive presence by replacing busyness, overwork, and boring communication with better judgment, clarity, and memorable ideas

Play the episode to discover what you can stop doing this week to create more influence, clearer decisions, and stronger executive presence—without simply working harder.

If you know you’re ready for the next level in your career—but you’re not sure whether your executive presence is helping you get there or quietly holding you back—start with the Executive Presence Scorecard.

This quick self-assessment will help you pinpoint where you’re already showing up as a confident, credible leader and where there may be gaps in how you communicate, influence, and lead.

Go to the show notes, click the link for the Executive Presence Scorecard, and take the assessment today. Your next level of leadership starts with knowing exactly where you stand.

To learn more visit www.speakupwithlaura.com. New Speak Up podcast episodes come out every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday early in the morning.

The Speak Up Podcast helps high-performing professionals develop executive presence through strategic communication, executive confidence, and leadership influence. Each episode provides practical strategies to help you speak up in meetings, communicate with senior leaders, present ideas with clarity, build executive visibility, strengthen your leadership presence, influence without authority, stop overexplaining, answer difficult questions with confidence, and become a trusted executive leader.

Whether you're preparing for your next Vice President promotion or looking to communicate with greater credibility and gravitas, you'll learn actionable executive communication skills that accelerate career growth.

Topics covered in this episode:

How to strengthen executive presence by communicating less
Why overexplaining can weaken your executive influence
How senior leaders prioritize information for better decision-making
Asking strategic questions instead of always having the answer
How productive disagreement builds leadership influence
Using storytelling to make executive communication more memorable
Moving from subject-matter expert to trusted executive advisor
Common high-performer habits that hurt executive presence
